The system includes synchronization circuitry, a first interrogator, and a second interrogator. The synchronization circuitry is configured to provide radio-frequency (RF) signal synthesis information that is used by both interrogators to coordinate the generation of RF signals.

The first interrogator receives the RF signal synthesis information from the synchronization circuitry and uses that information to generate a first RF signal for transmission toward a target device. In response, the first interrogator receives a second RF signal from the target device. The first interrogator then mixes the transmitted first RF signal with the received second RF signal to produce information related to the distance between the first interrogator and the target device.

The second interrogator also receives and uses the same RF signal synthesis information from the synchronization circuitry. Based on that shared information, the second interrogator generates a third RF signal for transmission toward the target device. The second interrogator receives a fourth RF signal from the target device and mixes the third RF signal with the fourth RF signal to determine information related to the distance between the second interrogator and the target device.

By using common RF signal synthesis information, the first and second interrogators can operate in a synchronized manner, allowing each interrogator to generate RF signals and derive distance-related information from signals received from the target device.
outputs.L4:
A synchronized RF interrogation system may include two or more interrogators that operate in a coordinated manner to determine range information for a target device. Each interrogator is configured to transmit an RF interrogation signal, receive an RF response signal from the target device, and process the received response using RF signal synthesis information that is shared or synchronized between the interrogators. The shared RF signal synthesis information may include, for example, frequency, phase, timing, modulation, chirp, sweep, or reference-clock information used to generate RF signals at the interrogators.

In operation, a first interrogator generates a first RF signal based on the shared synthesis information and transmits the signal toward the target device. The target device receives the transmitted signal and produces a response, such as a reflected, retransmitted, backscattered, or otherwise generated RF response. The first interrogator receives this response and mixes it with a locally generated RF signal that is also based on the shared synthesis information. The mixing operation produces an intermediate, beat, or difference-frequency signal whose characteristics correspond to the propagation delay between the first interrogator and the target device. From this delay, the distance between the first interrogator and the target device can be determined.

A second interrogator performs a similar operation. It generates or uses a synchronized local RF signal based on the same shared synthesis information, receives a response associated with the target device, and mixes the received RF signal with the locally generated RF signal. The resulting mixed RF signal provides information corresponding to the distance between the second interrogator and the target device. Because the interrogators use synchronized RF synthesis information, the measurements obtained at the different interrogators can be compared, combined, or otherwise processed in a common timing or phase reference framework.

The system may therefore determine separate range measurements from each interrogator to the target device. These range measurements may be used to coordinate interrogation activity, verify the presence or identity of the target device, improve measurement accuracy, or estimate the location of the target device. For example, when the positions of the interrogators are known, the distances from the interrogators to the target device may be used to localize the target device by multilateration, triangulation, or another range-based positioning technique. In this way, the synchronized RF interrogation system enables coordinated range measurement and localization using mixed RF signals produced from synchronized transmitted, received, and locally generated RF signals.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps us refer to something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we mean a particular book, not just any book.

Although “the” may seem simple, it gives clarity and precision to sentences. It can point to something already mentioned, something unique, or something known by both the speaker and the listener. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the best day” show how this tiny word can add meaning and focus.

In writing and speech, “the” helps organize ideas and guide understanding. Without it, many sentences would sound incomplete or confusing. This shows that even the smallest words can have a big impact on language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise patent abstract describing a system comprising synchronization circuitry, a first interrogator, and a second interrogator for determining distances to a target device using RF signals and mixed RF outputs.
counterfactuals.output: A system for determining distances to a target device includes synchronization circuitry, a first interrogator, and a second interrogator. The synchronization circuitry provides a timing reference to coordinate operation of the interrogators. The first interrogator transmits a first RF signal to the target device and receives a corresponding RF response, and the second interrogator transmits a second RF signal to the target device and receives a corresponding RF response. Each interrogator mixes a transmitted RF signal with a received RF signal to generate a mixed RF output indicative of propagation delay. Processing circuitry determines respective distances between the target device and the first and second interrogators based on the mixed RF outputs and the timing reference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please draft a single-paragraph patent disclosure for an RF distance measurement system in which a master synchronization circuit coordinates a transmitting/receiving interrogator and a receive-only interrogator that each use RF synthesis information to determine range to a target device.
counterfactuals.output: An RF distance measurement system includes a master synchronization circuit operably coupled to a transmitting/receiving interrogator and a receive-only interrogator, wherein the master synchronization circuit distributes timing, trigger, clock, phase-reference, or frequency-control information to coordinate range-measurement operations between the interrogators. The transmitting/receiving interrogator includes an RF synthesizer configured to generate one or more interrogation signals according to RF synthesis information, such as frequency, phase, chirp slope, hop sequence, modulation timing, or waveform-identification data, and transmits the interrogation signal toward a target device while also receiving a response, reflection, retransmission, or backscatter signal from the target device. The receive-only interrogator is positioned at a location spaced from the transmitting/receiving interrogator and includes a receiver and associated RF synthesis circuitry or synthesis-data interface configured to receive the signal associated with the target device without transmitting an interrogation signal. The master synchronization circuit causes the interrogators to use correlated RF synthesis information and a common time or phase reference so that received signal measurements at the transmitting/receiving interrogator and the receive-only interrogator can be compared or jointly processed. A processor determines a range, range difference, time-of-flight, phase-based distance, frequency-slope-derived distance, or multilateration parameter for the target device based at least in part on the RF synthesis information and received-signal information from both interrogators, thereby enabling distance determination using a coordinated active interrogator and a passive receive-only interrogator while reducing ambiguity caused by independent oscillator drift, timing skew, or uncontrolled RF waveform generation.
